chapters.title: Present simple vs present continuous
chapters.summary: Use present simple for routines and general truths, and present continuous for actions in progress or temporary situations.
points: Present simple describes habits and general truths.
Present continuous describes actions happening now.
Present continuous can describe temporary situations.

examples.english: She works in London.
She is working from home this week.

pitfalls: Do not overuse present continuous with stative verbs.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write three sentence pairs contrasting present simple and present continuous.

chapters.title: Present simple vs present continuous (2)
chapters.summary: Some stative verbs usually prefer the present simple, but the continuous can sometimes be used to emphasize temporariness or change.
points: Many state verbs are more commonly used in the present simple.
The present continuous can highlight temporary behavior or change.

examples.english: I understand the problem.
He is being difficult today.

pitfalls: Not every verb that describes a state sounds natural in the continuous.

practicePrompts.prompt: Rewrite five sentences using the more natural tense.

chapters.title: Future perfect vs future continuous
chapters.summary: Use the future perfect for actions completed before a future point, and the future continuous for actions in progress at that future time.
points: The future perfect focuses on completion before a future deadline.
The future continuous describes an activity that will be in progress at a specific future moment.
Both forms are useful when giving project updates and planning schedules.

examples.english: By Friday, the team will have finished the draft report.
At 10 a.m. tomorrow, the team will be presenting the proposal.
examples.note: action in progress at a future time

pitfalls: Do not use the future perfect when the meaning is simply a scheduled future action still in progress.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write four sentences about a project timeline using both the future perfect and the future continuous.

chapters.title: Mixed conditionals
chapters.summary: Mixed conditionals connect a hypothetical past event with a present result, or a present unreal condition with a past consequence.
points: Use a past unreal clause plus a present result when a different past action would change the current situation.
Use a present unreal clause plus a past result when a different present state would have changed an earlier outcome.
Mixed conditionals are common in reflection, analysis, and professional post-mortems.

examples.english: If we had prepared earlier, we would be in a stronger position now.
If she were more confident, she would have accepted the offer last week.

pitfalls: Do not use a mixed conditional when the sentence simply refers to a past result with no present consequence.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write four sentences using mixed conditionals to reflect on missed opportunities or present consequences.

chapters.title: Inversion for emphasis
chapters.summary: Formal inversion is used after negative adverbials and limiting expressions to create emphasis and a more advanced written style.
points: Inversion often follows expressions like rarely, never, only then, and not until.
The auxiliary usually comes before the subject when inversion is required.
This pattern is common in formal reports, commentary, and argumentative writing.

examples.english: Rarely have I seen a team respond so quickly to a crisis.
Only after the review did the managers approve the revised plan.

pitfalls: Do not invert after every adverbial; the structure is limited to specific emphatic patterns.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write four formal sentences that use inversion for emphasis after negative or limiting expressions.

chapters.title: Applying for a job
chapters.summary: Vocabulary for job ads, cover letters, applications and career-related language.
points: A cover letter should highlight relevant experience and suitability for the role.
Job ads often mention career prospects, training and salary expectations.
Applications should stand out clearly and professionally.

examples.english: Please find attached my CV in support of my application.
The post offers excellent career prospects.

pitfalls: Do not confuse a cover letter with a CV.
Avoid overly casual language in job applications.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write a short cover letter for an entry-level role.
List five phrases commonly used in job advertisements.

chapters.title: Job interviews
chapters.summary: Vocabulary and phrases used in job interviews, including preparation, confidence, first impressions, interview panels and job offers.
points: Candidates may be shortlisted for interview based on selection criteria.
It is important to do your homework before an interview.
Body language and first impressions matter.
Candidates may be asked about previous roles, responsibilities and notice period.
A job offer may include salary, benefits and reporting structure.

examples.english: I was shortlisted for an interview last week.
We believe your qualifications are an ideal fit for the role.
My notice period is two weeks.

pitfalls: Do not confuse a line manager with an interview panel.
Do not use overly casual language when discussing experience in an interview.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write five interview questions and model answers.
Describe a previous role using formal interview language.
Draft a short acceptance email for a job offer.

chapters.title: Job ad analysis
chapters.summary: Reading practice focused on identifying the main offer, required profile and overall tone in a job advertisement.
points: Strong job ads explain the role, training and career prospects clearly.
Candidates should identify the required profile and the benefits that are being emphasized.
The tone is usually persuasive but professional.

examples.english: The post offers excellent career prospects and structured training.

pitfalls: Do not confuse the core responsibilities with the optional benefits.

practicePrompts.prompt: CityBridge Consulting is looking for a junior operations assistant to support client projects, coordinate schedules, and prepare internal reports. The role includes structured training, regular mentoring, and clear career progression for candidates who show initiative. Applicants should have strong communication skills, good attention to detail, and the ability to work calmly under pressure. Previous internship experience is helpful, but we are mainly looking for people who learn quickly and write professionally.

chapters.title: Interview panel summary
chapters.summary: Listening practice focused on the final decision and contrasting details in an interview discussion.
points: The panel values strong preparation and clear examples from previous roles.
One interviewer is impressed by the candidate's communication skills, but another worries about limited leadership experience.
The final position is positive overall, although the panel wants one more example of handling deadlines.

examples.english: She gave clear examples from her previous role, but the panel still asked for more detail about deadlines.

pitfalls: Do not miss the final recommendation just because one concern is mentioned along the way.

practicePrompts.prompt: The panel agrees that the candidate communicated confidently and gave strong examples from her customer service role, but one interviewer notes that she did not fully explain how she manages multiple deadlines. In the end, the panel decides to move her to the next stage because her preparation and communication are stronger than those of the other candidates.

chapters.title: Interview self-introduction
chapters.summary: Speaking practice focused on introducing previous experience and strengths in an interview.
points: A strong interview introduction should identify the previous role, key responsibilities, and one relevant strength.
Candidates should connect experience to the role they are applying for.
A clear connector helps the answer sound more fluent and structured.

examples.english: In my previous role, I supported customer projects and learned how to communicate clearly under pressure.

pitfalls: Do not give a list of unrelated facts without explaining why they matter for the role.

practicePrompts.prompt: You are in a job interview. Introduce your previous role, describe two responsibilities, and explain one strength that makes you a good fit for the position.

chapters.title: Meeting minutes analysis
chapters.summary: Reading practice focused on tracing decisions, reservations and action points in formal meeting minutes.
points: Meeting minutes usually separate the final decision from background discussion.
A reservation or condition can change the practical meaning of an approved plan.
Action points reveal who owns the next steps after the meeting.

examples.english: The committee approved the phased rollout, subject to additional support training.

pitfalls: Do not confuse a proposed idea with the final approved decision.

practicePrompts.prompt: The minutes note that the team approved a phased product launch for July, provided the support team receives extra training by mid-June. Marketing asked for a wider campaign, but the chair decided to keep the first release limited to three markets so that technical issues could be handled more carefully. The final action items assign training materials to the support lead and customer-facing FAQs to marketing.

chapters.title: Deadline renegotiation call
chapters.summary: Listening practice focused on the final agreement and the main concern raised in a deadline negotiation.
points: A negotiation may end positively even when one side raises a serious concern.
The speaker's final agreement is often qualified by one condition or monitoring step.
Deadline language often combines reassurance with a request for interim updates.

examples.english: We can accept the revised date, but we will need a progress update by Tuesday.

pitfalls: Do not focus only on the delay itself and miss the condition attached to the new deadline.

practicePrompts.prompt: The client says they understand the technical issue that delayed the release and are willing to accept a revised delivery date of 18 June. However, they stress that the project cannot slip again because the board review is scheduled for the following week. The call ends with an agreement that the team will send a written progress update by Tuesday and confirm final testing by Friday.

chapters.title: Project update briefing
chapters.summary: Speaking practice focused on concise project updates that balance completed work, current progress and one active risk.
points: A strong project briefing explains what has been completed before moving to current tasks.
Managers expect at least one risk or dependency to be flagged clearly.
Connectors help the update sound structured rather than improvised.

examples.english: We have completed the first testing cycle, and we are now preparing the client-facing documentation.

pitfalls: Do not give a list of disconnected tasks without explaining the current risk or next step.

practicePrompts.prompt: Give a short project update to a manager. Mention what has been completed, what is still in progress, and one risk that needs attention.

chapters.title: Delay update email
chapters.summary: Writing practice focused on explaining a delay, maintaining a professional tone and proposing a revised plan.
points: A good delay update names the problem clearly without sounding defensive.
Professional emails should explain the revised plan and next checkpoint.
The tone should remain calm, responsible and solution-focused.

examples.english: Unfortunately, the client pack will be ready one day later than planned, but we will send the revised version by Thursday afternoon.

pitfalls: Do not apologize repeatedly without explaining the revised plan and next step.

practicePrompts.prompt: Write a short professional email explaining a delivery delay, the reason for it, and the revised plan.
